explanations.answer: He will not be consulted by them
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. The elders sat down expecting a word, and God says, "As surely as I live, I will not be consulted by you…" (Ezekiel 20:3). He backs it with an oath on His own life. Those elders walked in with a question and got a closed door, and I'd be checking my pockets for my keys.

Oh, those elders would have LOVED a "come back tomorrow." But there's no tomorrow in what God says. He says, "As surely as I live, I will not be consulted by you…" (Ezekiel 20:3). The answer is no, and He swears to it.

explanations.answer: He will answer them in a dream
explanations.explanation: No dream shows up here, friend. The word of the LORD comes to Ezekiel, and the message is that God will not be consulted by these elders. He says it with an oath, "As surely as I live…" (Ezekiel 20:3). So there's no side door for them to try.

explanations.answer: Bring them out into a land He picked for them
explanations.explanation: That's it. God swore to bring them out of Egypt into a land He had searched out for them. He calls it a land flowing with milk and honey, the glory of all lands (Ezekiel 20:6). He didn't just pick a spot. He went looking.

explanations.answer: Give them the best land in all of Egypt
explanations.explanation: Close, but the oath points the other way. God swore to bring them OUT of the land of Egypt. The land He promised was one He had searched out for them, flowing with milk and honey (Ezekiel 20:6). Egypt was where they were leaving.

explanations.answer: Make them the rulers over all of Egypt
explanations.explanation: That's a big promise, but it's not the one on the page. God swore to bring them out of Egypt into a land He had searched out for them (Ezekiel 20:6). Nothing here says they would rule Egypt. The plan was to take them OUT.

Right on the money. God tells them, "…you must not defile yourselves with the idols of Egypt. I am the LORD your God." (Ezekiel 20:7). Throw away the abominations before your eyes, and stay clear of Egypt's idols. He says who He is right alongside the command.

Bricks are a fun guess, but they're not in this verse. God names the idols of Egypt as the thing they must not defile themselves with (Ezekiel 20:7). He's talking about what they worship, not what they build with.
No gold in this command, friend. The verse says they must not defile themselves with the idols of Egypt (Ezekiel 20:7). It's about what they bow down to, not what they own.

True. God says, "None of them cast away the abominations before their eyes, and they did not forsake the idols of Egypt." (Ezekiel 20:8). Not a few of them. NONE of them. That's about as complete as it gets.

The text says it plainly: "None of them cast away the abominations before their eyes…" (Ezekiel 20:8). So the statement is true. God had told each of them to throw those things away, and not one did. It's a hard line, but that's what's written.

explanations.answer: The nations they were living among
explanations.explanation: Yes. God acted so His name would not be profaned in the eyes of the nations among whom they were living (Ezekiel 20:9). Those nations had seen Him reveal Himself to Israel by bringing them out of Egypt. His name was on the line in front of them.

Angels are a nice thought, but this verse doesn't mention them. It says God acted so His name would not be profaned in the eyes of the nations among whom they were living (Ezekiel 20:9). Those were the watchers, because He had revealed Himself in their sight.

explanations.answer: The elders of their own tribes
explanations.explanation: The text points somewhere else, friend. God says He acted so His name would not be profaned in the eyes of the nations among whom they were living (Ezekiel 20:9). Those nations had watched Him bring Israel out of Egypt. The tribal elders aren't named in that verse.

explanations.answer: So they'd know He's the LORD who makes them holy
explanations.explanation: That's the purpose God gives. He says the Sabbaths are "a sign between us, so that they would know that I am the LORD who sanctifies them." (Ezekiel 20:12). Sanctifies means He's the one who makes them holy. The Sabbath was a reminder of who was doing the work.

explanations.answer: So they'd know when to plant and when to harvest
explanations.explanation: Good practical guess, but that's not the reason on the page. God gives the Sabbaths as a sign between Him and them, so they would know He is the LORD who sanctifies them (Ezekiel 20:12). The sign is about who He is to them.

explanations.answer: So their enemies would be afraid of them
explanations.explanation: No enemies in this verse, friend. The Sabbaths are a sign between God and Israel, so they would know that He is the LORD who sanctifies them (Ezekiel 20:12). It's about their relationship with Him.

The text says the opposite. "…the house of Israel rebelled against Me in the wilderness. They did not follow My statutes and they rejected My ordinances…and they utterly profaned My Sabbaths." (Ezekiel 20:13). So the statement is false. God gave good things, and they turned from them.

False is right. God says they did not follow His statutes, they rejected His ordinances, and they utterly profaned His Sabbaths (Ezekiel 20:13). He even repeats that the man who does these things will live by them. They had the gift in their hands and walked away from it.

Yes, the land. God swore He would not bring that generation into "the land that I had given them—a land flowing with milk and honey, the glory of all lands—" (Ezekiel 20:15). It's the same land He had picked out for them. That oath is a heavy one.
A temple isn't in this verse, friend. God swears He will not bring them into the land He had given them, a land flowing with milk and honey (Ezekiel 20:15). It's the land that's on the line.

Kingdom sounds grand, but the verse uses a plainer word. God swears He will not bring them into the land He had given them, a land flowing with milk and honey, the glory of all lands (Ezekiel 20:15). It's the same promised land from the start.
That's the one. God says it was because "their hearts continually went after their idols." (Ezekiel 20:16). The problem started deep inside. And notice the word continually.
Hands would be easy to blame, friend, but the verse goes deeper. God says their hearts continually went after their idols (Ezekiel 20:16). It's about where their wanting was pointed.
Tongues get blamed for a lot, but not here. The verse says their hearts continually went after their idols (Ezekiel 20:16). That's the reason God gives for the oath.

That's not what the text says. God says, "Yet I looked on them with pity and did not destroy them or bring them to an end in the wilderness." (Ezekiel 20:17). So the statement is false. They had rebelled over and over, and still He held back.

False is right. God says, "Yet I looked on them with pity and did not destroy them or bring them to an end in the wilderness." (Ezekiel 20:17). They had earned a hard oath about the land, but He did not end them. Pity is the word the verse uses.

Right. God says to the children, "I am the LORD your God; walk in My statutes, keep My ordinances, and practice them." (Ezekiel 20:19). First He says what not to follow, then He says what to follow. His own word is the path.
The elders aren't part of this instruction, friend. God says to the children, "…walk in My statutes, keep My ordinances, and practice them." (Ezekiel 20:19). The statutes He points to are His own.

Making up their own rules would be tempting, but God doesn't say that. He says, "I am the LORD your God; walk in My statutes, keep My ordinances, and practice them." (Ezekiel 20:19). The statutes are His, not theirs.

The text says otherwise. "But the children rebelled against Me. They did not walk in My statutes or carefully observe My ordinances…" (Ezekiel 20:21). So the statement is false. The children went the same direction their fathers did.

False is right. God says the children did not walk in His statutes or carefully observe His ordinances, and they profaned His Sabbaths (Ezekiel 20:21). He had told them what to do and what to avoid. They rebelled anyway.

explanations.answer: He'll scatter them among the nations
explanations.explanation: That's the oath. God swears He would "scatter them among the nations and disperse them throughout the lands." (Ezekiel 20:23). The reason He gives is that they rejected His statutes, profaned His Sabbaths and fixed their eyes on their fathers' idols (Ezekiel 20:24). It's a serious oath.

explanations.answer: He'll make them a great empire
explanations.explanation: That's the opposite direction, friend. God swears He would scatter them among the nations and disperse them throughout the lands (Ezekiel 20:23). Scattered is a long way from an empire.

explanations.answer: He'll send them back to Egypt
explanations.explanation: Back to Egypt isn't in the oath. God swears He would scatter them among the nations and disperse them throughout the lands (Ezekiel 20:23). The oath is about being spread out, not turned around.

explanations.answer: On any high hill or under any leafy tree
explanations.explanation: That's what the text says. "…they saw any high hill or leafy tree, there they offered their sacrifices…" (Ezekiel 20:28). They also presented offerings, sent up incense and poured out drink offerings. Any nice-looking hill or shady tree was enough.

explanations.answer: Only at the altar God chose for them
explanations.explanation: The text says the opposite. They offered their sacrifices wherever they saw any high hill or leafy tree (Ezekiel 20:28). So it wasn't only one place. They went all over.

explanations.answer: In the courts of the LORD's house
explanations.explanation: Not in the verse, friend. When they came into the land and saw any high hill or leafy tree, there they offered their sacrifices (Ezekiel 20:28). It's the hills and trees that are named.

Yes, provoked. God says they "presented offerings that provoked Me…" (Ezekiel 20:28). They were sending up incense and pouring out drink offerings, and it provoked Him. Offerings can be given the wrong way.
The verse says the opposite. These offerings "provoked Me" (Ezekiel 20:28). They were presenting them on every hill and under every leafy tree. God was not pleased by them.
They may have thought they were honoring Him, but that's not what God says. He says they presented offerings "that provoked Me" (Ezekiel 20:28). So the word is provoked.

Bamah it is. God asks, "What is this high place to which you go?" and the verse adds, "(And to this day it is called Bamah.)" (Ezekiel 20:29). The name stuck, and it was still the name when this was written.
Bethel is a real place name, but it's not the one this verse gives. It says the high place "to this day…is called Bamah." (Ezekiel 20:29). Bamah is the name that stuck.
Gilgal's a good guess, friend, but the verse names a different one. It says, "(And to this day it is called Bamah.)" (Ezekiel 20:29). Bamah is what the high place was called.
True. God says, "…you continue to defile yourselves with all your idols to this day." (Ezekiel 20:31). It wasn't only their fathers. Right up to the day Ezekiel spoke, the same habit was going on.
The text says otherwise. God tells them, "…you continue to defile yourselves with all your idols to this day." (Ezekiel 20:31). So the statement is true. It wasn't just old history.

That's it. They say, "Let us be like the nations, like the peoples of the lands, serving wood and stone…" (Ezekiel 20:32). Wood and stone are the idols they wanted to serve. God answers what they have in mind.
Kings and armies aren't in what they say. They say, "Let us be like the nations…serving wood and stone…" (Ezekiel 20:32). The talk is about idols.
Sun and moon aren't mentioned here, friend. What they say is, "…serving wood and stone…" (Ezekiel 20:32). Wood and stone are what they'd be serving.
God says the opposite. "…what you have in mind will never come to pass." (Ezekiel 20:32). So the statement is false. They wanted to blend in with the nations, and God says no.
False is right. God says, "…what you have in mind will never come to pass." (Ezekiel 20:32). Never is a strong word. Their plan to be like the nations is not going to happen.

Gather is right. God says, "With a strong hand, an outstretched arm, and outpoured wrath I will bring you out from the peoples and gather you from the lands to which you have been scattered." (Ezekiel 20:34). The same hand that scatters is the hand that gathers.
Forget isn't the word, friend. God says He will bring them out from the peoples and "gather you from the lands to which you have been scattered." (Ezekiel 20:34). He's bringing them back together.
Nobody's being sold here. God says He will bring them out from the peoples and "gather you from the lands to which you have been scattered." (Ezekiel 20:34). Gathering is what He promises.

explanations.answer: Enter into judgment face to face
explanations.explanation: That's what He says. "…I will bring you into the wilderness of the nations, where I will enter into judgment with you face to face." (Ezekiel 20:35). Face to face means no middleman. It's just God and His people.
Hiding isn't in this verse. God says He will bring them into the wilderness of the nations, "where I will enter into judgment with you face to face." (Ezekiel 20:35). It's a judgment meeting.

explanations.answer: Lead them by a pillar of fire
explanations.explanation: A pillar of fire isn't mentioned in this passage, friend. What God says is that He will enter into judgment with them face to face in the wilderness of the nations (Ezekiel 20:35).

That's not what God says. He says, "I will purge you of those who rebel and transgress against Me. I will bring them out of the land in which they dwell, but they will not enter the land of Israel." (Ezekiel 20:38). So the statement is false. The rebels don't make it in.

False is right. God says He will bring the rebels out of the land where they live, "but they will not enter the land of Israel." (Ezekiel 20:38). Then the people will know He is the LORD. Those who rebel are purged out.

explanations.answer: They will surely listen to Him
explanations.explanation: Yes. God says, "Go and serve your idols, every one of you. But afterward, you will surely listen to Me…" (Ezekiel 20:39). Surely is a strong word. The story doesn't end with the idols.

explanations.answer: They will forget Him for good
explanations.explanation: That's the opposite of what God says. After they go serve their idols, He says, "But afterward, you will surely listen to Me…" (Ezekiel 20:39). So they won't forget Him for good.

explanations.answer: They will go back to Egypt
explanations.explanation: Egypt doesn't come up here, friend. God says, "But afterward, you will surely listen to Me…" (Ezekiel 20:39). Listening is what comes next.

That's the spot. God says, "For on My holy mountain, the high mountain of Israel, declares the Lord GOD, there the whole house of Israel, all of them, will serve Me in the land." (Ezekiel 20:40). The whole house of Israel, all of them. Nobody's left out.

Egypt is where they started, friend, but it's not where this promise lands. God says the whole house of Israel will serve Him on His holy mountain, the high mountain of Israel (Ezekiel 20:40). It's "in the land."

Rivers of Babylon aren't in this verse. God says, "For on My holy mountain, the high mountain of Israel…there the whole house of Israel, all of them, will serve Me in the land." (Ezekiel 20:40). His holy mountain is the place.

True, and what a turn. He says, "There I will accept them and will require your offerings and choice gifts, along with all your holy sacrifices." (Ezekiel 20:40). The One who said He would not be consulted now says He will accept them. Same God, new chapter for His people.
The text says otherwise. On His holy mountain God says, "There I will accept them…" (Ezekiel 20:40). So the statement is true. After all the refusals, He promises acceptance.

Aroma is right. God says, "I will accept you as a pleasing aroma." (Ezekiel 20:41). Sort of like when the whole house smells like a fresh batch and everybody wanders into the kitchen. Same scent, different promise.
A melody is a nice idea, friend, but the verse uses a different word. God says, "I will accept you as a pleasing aroma." (Ezekiel 20:41). It's something you smell, not something you hear.
No garden in this one. God says He will accept them "as a pleasing aroma." (Ezekiel 20:41). They'll be gathered from the lands where they were scattered.

That's what the text says. "There you will remember your ways and all the deeds with which you have defiled yourselves, and you will loathe yourselves for all the evils you have done." (Ezekiel 20:43). It's a heavy line. They finally see their ways for what they were.

explanations.answer: They will be proud of themselves
explanations.explanation: It goes the other way. God says they will remember their ways and "loathe yourselves for all the evils you have done." (Ezekiel 20:43). No pride shows up in that moment.

God doesn't say that, friend. He says, "There you will remember your ways and all the deeds with which you have defiled yourselves, and you will loathe yourselves…" (Ezekiel 20:43). They look at their own ways.

Wicked is the word. God says, "…when I have dealt with you for the sake of My name and not according to your wicked ways and corrupt acts, declares the Lord GOD." (Ezekiel 20:44). He deals with them for the sake of His name. He doesn't deal with them according to their ways.
Ancient isn't the word, friend. God says, "…not according to your wicked ways and corrupt acts…" (Ezekiel 20:44). He's talking about what they did, not how old it was.

Careful is almost a joke, baker, because careful is exactly what they weren't. The verse says, "…not according to your wicked ways and corrupt acts…" (Ezekiel 20:44). God deals with them for the sake of His name.
